definition: In a right-angled triangle, the sine of an angle is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse, written $\sin\theta$. A calculator or the sine graph gives it for any angle, such as $150^{\circ}$.

In a right-angled triangle, the cosine of an angle is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse, written $\cos\theta$. A calculator or the cosine graph gives it for any angle, such as $150^{\circ}$.

In a right-angled triangle, the tangent of an angle is the opposite side divided by the adjacent side, written $\tan\theta$. A calculator or the tangent graph gives it for any angle except $90^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$ and so on. It is not the same as a tangent line to a circle or curve.
In a right-angled triangle, the side directly across from the angle you are working with; it does not touch that angle.
In a right-angled triangle, the side that touches the angle you are working with and is not the hypotenuse.
The angle you look up through from the horizontal to see something higher; looking down from the horizontal gives an angle of depression instead.
